spans.content: REAP: Relation-Aware Elicitation and Parsing
for Closed-Book Knowledge Base Construction from LLMs
Thanh-Dan Bui Thanh-Trung Do Tuan-Phong Nguyen
VNU University of Engineering and Technology, Hanoi, Vietnam
{23020342, 24022472, tuanphong}@vnu.edu.vn
Abstract
We present the REAP system for the AKBC
Shared Task 2026 on constructing knowledge
bases from language models in a closed-book
setting, subject to a budget of at most 32B pa-
rameters and no model fine-tuning. Our system
combines structured chain-of-thought reason-
ing, relation-specific query strategies, and a
reasoning-based empty-set gate to elicit para-
metric knowledge, followed by direct extrac-
tion into valid JSON arrays. On the official
test set, the system, built on Mistral-Small-
24B-Instruct-2501, achieves a macro-F1 score
of 0.62, with particularly strong results on
countryLandBordersCountry (F = 0.95),
companyTradesAtStockExchange (F
0.73), and hasArea (F = 0.77). Our code
is publicly available.<sup>1</sup>
1 Introduction
Large language models (LLMs) encode substan-
tial factual knowledge in their parameters (Petroni
et al., 2019). However, eliciting this knowledge
for knowledge base construction (KBC) is consid-
erably more challenging than answering isolated
factual questions: a subject–relation pair (s, r) may
correspond to an empty (∅), single-valued (1), or
multi-valued (N) object set. The AKBC Shared
Task 2026 (Kalo et al., 2026) formalizes this prob-
lem under a constrained setting: systems must op-
erate in a closed-book fashion, without retrieval-
augmented generation or external knowledge; use
at most 32B parameters; and perform no model
fine-tuning.
In this task, each input record specifies a sub-
ject entity and one of the six given relations (see
Table 1), and the system must return the complete
set of corresponding objects as a valid JSON array.
The relations cover geographic adjacency and area,
a person’s city of death, venue capacity, award re-
cipients, and the stock exchanges on which a com-
pany is traded. Consequently, the required output
may be empty, contain a single object, or contain
a long list of objects, while quantitative answers
must also be sufficiently precise. Table 1 summa-
rizes the six target relations and the scope of their
ground-truth labels.
Earlier factual probing methods use cloze-style
prompts or prompt ensembles to rank candidate ob-
jects (Petroni et al., 2019; Jiang et al., 2020), while
the LM-KBC challenge series additionally requires
systems to materialize variable-cardinality answer
sets (Singhania et al., 2022; Kalo et al., 2023, 2024,
2025). A direct generative solution that asks the
model to recall all objects and produce correctly
formatted JSON in a single pass can therefore hal-
lucinate objects, omit valid answers, or violate the
output schema.
To address this issue, we propose REAP
(Relation-aware Elicitation And Parsing), a two-
stage pipeline that decouples factual elicitation
from answer serialization. Stage 1 prompts the
LLM using strategies tailored to each relation,
whereas Stage 2 uses deterministic JSON pars-
ing when possible and LLM-based extraction only
as a fallback. This separation allows the model to
focus on recalling the answer set before the system
enforces the required JSON format.
Our main contributions are as follows:
1. Relation-Aware Elicitation: We design spe-
cialized strategies for different relation types,
including CoT reasoning with an empty-set
gate, a four-direction geographical scan for
land borders, and chronological multi-pass
querying for awards.

parsing handles approximately 80% of the
records, while LLM-based extraction is re-

2 Related Work
Probing knowledge in language models.
LAMA (Petroni et al., 2019) established cloze-
style probing but assumes exactly one object per
relation, and what can be extracted depends heavily
on the prompt (Jiang et al., 2020); see AlKhamissi
et al. (2022) for a survey. The LM-KBC challenge
series (Singhania et al., 2022; Kalo et al., 2023,
2024, 2025) recast this as knowledge base con-
struction with arbitrary-cardinality object sets (0, 1,
or N), the setting continued by the AKBC Shared
Task 2026 (Kalo et al., 2026). Prior systems pair
LLM probing with entity mapping (Zhang et al.,
2023); most recently, ReWiSe (Albert-Roulhac
and Zouaq, 2025), a top-performing system at
LM-KBC 2025, combines chain-of-thought (CoT)
reasoning with relation-wise self-consistency.
In REAP, we adopt the idea of relation-specific
CoT and explicit empty-set handling, but drop
self-consistency voting, which is costly and can be
dominated by confident-but-incorrect reasoning
chains.
Parametric knowledge and its limits. Closed-
book QA shows that language models can an-
swer factual questions without retrieval (Roberts
et al., 2020), motivating the closed-book setting we
adopt. This parametric knowledge is uneven, how-
ever: models recall popular facts well but struggle
with long-tail entities (Kandpal et al., 2023; Mallen
et al., 2023), which bounds any closed-book system
and matches our error analysis on rare subjects.
Step-by-step reasoning and empty-set gate.
Chain-of-thought prompting (Wei et al., 2022; Ko-
jima et al., 2022) improves multi-step reasoning
and builds on the in-context learning ability of
instruction-tuned LLMs (Brown et al., 2020). Since
a correct answer may itself be the empty set, in
REAP, we add a reasoning-based empty-set gate in-
spired by selective prediction (Kamath et al., 2020).
Unlike calibrated methods that estimate whether a
model knows an answer (Kadavath et al., 2022),
our gate is a prompt-driven decision that returns
an empty set as the final answer when the property
does not exist or the evidence of it is insufficient.

Stage 1 prompts are specialized per relation
following three principles: (i) query decom-
position to maximize recall on multi-valued
relations (e.g., six decade-scoped passes for
awardWonBy and a four-direction geographi-
cal scan for countryLandBordersCountry); (ii)
output-format constraints via BORDERS: or
FINAL_ANSWER: [. . . ] markers; and (iii) step-
by-step reasoning with an empty-set gate that
outputs FINAL_ANSWER: [] for unanswerable en-
tities (e.g., living individuals or private companies).
Together, these relation-tailored, multi-step CoT
procedures constitute the structured reasoning that

awardWonBy: Chronological Multi-Pass. For
major awards with dozens or hundreds of recip-
ients, a single query typically yields low recall. We
therefore use a multi-pass strategy comprising one
general prompt and five auxiliary prompts decom-
posed chronologically: from the award’s inception
through the 1970s, the 1980s–1990s, the 2000s–
2010s, 2020 onward, and a final pass targeting less
prominent or non-Western recipients. All six gen-
erations use temperature T = 0.7 to diversify recall
before the evidence is merged.
countryLandBordersCountry: Four-Direction
Geographical Scan. The prompt instructs the
model to act as a geography expert and inspect the
subject’s eastern, western, southern, and northern
boundaries. This scan reduces omissions of small
neighboring countries and adjacent detached terri-
tories. The prompt includes land borders only, ex-
plicitly excludes maritime boundaries, and returns
BORDERS: NONE for island countries. If the re-
sponse lacks the BORDERS: marker, the system au-
tomatically retries with a shorter fallback prompt.
companyTradesAtStockExchange: Four-Step
Listing Check. The model follows a four-step
CoT procedure: (1) identify the company; (2) ap-
ply a Strict Public Check (empty-set gate) to
determine whether the entity is a private company,
a nonprofit organization, or a subsidiary that is
not separately listed, returning FINAL_ANSWER: []
if any condition holds; (3) retrieve all listing ex-
changes using their full official names, such as New
York Stock Exchange or SIX Swiss Exchange; and
(4) conclude with FINAL_ANSWER: ["Exchange
Name"].
hasArea: Four-Step Entity Disambiguation and
Unit Normalization. The model follows four
CoT steps: (1) distinguish the target entity (e.g., an
island, lake, or region) from the country containing
it; (2) retrieve its area from parametric knowledge
while preserving decimal precision; (3) convert the
value to km<sup>2</sup>; and (4) output an integer or decimal
value as FINAL_ANSWER: ["Value"].
hasCapacity: Four-Step Reasoning with
Capacity-Range Verification. The model fol-
lows four CoT steps: (1) determine the venue
type and location; (2) distinguish a university or
small local stadium from a larger national stadium
with a similar name or in the same city; (3) check
the estimate against a plausible capacity range
(1,000–35,000 seats for small venues and 35,000–
100,000 for large national stadiums); and (4) re-
turn the capacity as an integer in FINAL_ANSWER:
["Value"].

3.3 Post-processing
To ensure that extracted outputs adhere to the
ground-truth format, we apply the following auto-
mated post-processing procedure after the genera-
tion phase:
1. Direct Parsing and Robust Array Extrac-
tion: The system directly parses the con-
tent of the FINAL_ANSWER: line or recovers a
truncated JSON array using balanced-bracket
scanning.
2. Numeric Extraction and Normalization:
For quantitative relations (hasArea and
hasCapacity), regular expressions extract in-
teger or floating-point values while removing
thousands separators and measurement units.
3. Title and Noise Filtering: For awardWonBy,
the system removes year prefixes (e.g., "1938:
Albert Einstein"), HTML tags, work-title suf-
fixes, and honorifics such as Dr., Prof., Sir,
Dame, Lord, Saint, St., and Mr. to obtain nor-
malized entity names.
4. Parenthetical Filtering and Deduplica-
tion: The system removes trailing parenthet-
ical qualifiers (e.g., "Guinea (West Africa)"
→ "Guinea") and performs case-insensitive
deduplication while preserving the capitaliza-
tion of the first occurrence.
4 Experiments
4.1 Experimental Setup
Data. The organizers provide training, valida-
tion, and test splits for six relations. The validation
and test splits each contain 475 records: 68 for
countryLandBordersCountry in validation (67 in
test), 97 and 98 for hasCapacity respectively, 10
for awardWonBy, and 100 for each of the other three
relations. Each record consists of a subject, a re-
lation, and a set of objects, each accompanied by
a list of aliases. The data cover all three cardinal-
ity cases: empty sets (e.g., New Zealand for land
borders), single-valued relations, and multi-valued
relations (e.g., Nobel Prize in Physics, 229 recipi-
ents in train.jsonl, or AAAI Fellow, 350 people
in val.jsonl).
Models. We evaluate three instruction-tuned
models—Gemma-2-9B-it (Gemma Team, 2024),
Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (Llama Team, Meta AI,
2024), and Mistral-Small-24B-Instruct-2501 (Mis-
tral AI, 2025)—and compare against the orga-
nizer’s Qwen3.5-9B baseline (Qwen Team, 2026).
Gemma-2-9B-it and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct serve
as comparison systems, while Mistral-Small-24B-
Instruct-2501 (hereafter Mistral-24B) is the pri-
mary model in our final system.
Hardware and Runtime. Experiments are con-
ducted on Kaggle using a TPU v5e-8 with eight
TPU v5e cores. We serve the models with vLLM
TPU Server and use bfloat16 precision. With di-
rect parsing and batched inference, one complete
run over all six relations in the validation set (475
records) takes approximately 2–5 minutes with
batch_size=32.
Metrics. We report macro/micro precision,
recall, and F1 using the organizer-provided
evaluate.py script. For string-valued relations,
the evaluator normalizes predictions and matches
aliases through maximum bipartite matching. For
quantitative relations, it applies a relative tolerance
of 5%. Overall macro-F1 is the mean of the per-
record F1 scores.
4.2 Validation Results
We first evaluate all models in a zero-shot setting,
using direct queries without evidence generation
or CoT reasoning. As shown in Figure 2, Llama-
3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-24B achieve
macro-F1 scores of 0.38, 0.42, and 0.43, respec-
tively. These relatively low and similar scores sug-
gest that all three models struggle when required to
recall facts and satisfy the output format simultane-
ously. The limitation is particularly pronounced for
multi-valued relations that require long object lists,
such as awardWonBy, and for quantitative relations
requiring precise values.

nizer’s Qwen3.5-9B baseline (Qwen Team, 2026).
Gemma-2-9B-it and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct serve
as comparison systems, while Mistral-Small-24B-
Instruct-2501 (hereafter Mistral-24B) is the pri-
mary model in our final system.
Hardware and Runtime. Experiments are con-
ducted on Kaggle using a TPU v5e-8 with eight
TPU v5e cores. We serve the models with vLLM
TPU Server and use bfloat16 precision. With di-
rect parsing and batched inference, one complete
run over all six relations in the validation set (475
records) takes approximately 2–5 minutes with
batch_size=32.
Metrics. We report macro/micro precision,
recall, and F1 using the organizer-provided
evaluate.py script. For string-valued relations,
the evaluator normalizes predictions and matches
aliases through maximum bipartite matching. For
quantitative relations, it applies a relative tolerance
of 5%. Overall macro-F1 is the mean of the per-
record F1 scores.
4.2 Validation Results
We first evaluate all models in a zero-shot setting,
using direct queries without evidence generation
or CoT reasoning. As shown in Figure 2, Llama-
3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-24B achieve
macro-F1 scores of 0.38, 0.42, and 0.43, respec-
tively. These relatively low and similar scores sug-
gest that all three models struggle when required to
recall facts and satisfy the output format simultane-
ously. The limitation is particularly pronounced for
multi-valued relations that require long object lists,
such as awardWonBy, and for quantitative relations
requiring precise values.
Effectiveness of the Two-Stage Pipeline. Fig-
ure 2 shows that the two-stage pipeline im-
proves macro-F1 for all three models. Llama-
3.1-8B improves from 0.38 to 0.48, Gemma-2-9B
from 0.42 to 0.51, and Mistral-24B from 0.43 to
0.65. Mistral-24B yields the largest absolute gain
(+0.22) and is therefore selected as the primary
model in our final system submitted to the AKBC
Shared Task 2026.

To quantify each component’s contribution, we per-

Removing Task Decomposition drops macro-

Prompting. In the zero-shot setting, all models
exhibit limited and relatively similar performance.

lations with large object sets, such as awardWonBy,
and for quantitative relations that demand precise
values, such as hasArea and hasCapacity. Ap-
plying the complete two-stage pipeline of REAP
with relation-specific prompts, CoT reasoning, a
reasoning-based empty-set gate, and direct parsing
improves all three models. These results indicate
that structured reasoning is important for reliably
eliciting knowledge encoded in model parameters.

reveal a clear gap between the 9B model (Gemma-
2-9B) and the 24B model (Mistral-24B). In the
zero-shot setting, the models perform similarly,

6 Discussion
Relation-Aware Prompting versus Zero-Shot
Prompting. In the zero-shot setting, all models
exhibit limited and relatively similar performance.
Requiring a model to recall facts and produce valid
JSON in a single pass is especially difficult for re-
lations with large object sets, such as awardWonBy,
and for quantitative relations that demand precise
values, such as hasArea and hasCapacity. Ap-
plying the complete two-stage pipeline of REAP
with relation-specific prompts, CoT reasoning, a
reasoning-based empty-set gate, and direct parsing
improves all three models. These results indicate

eliciting knowledge encoded in model parameters.
Limits of Parametric Knowledge. Our results
reveal a clear gap between the 9B model (Gemma-
2-9B) and the 24B model (Mistral-24B). In the
zero-shot setting, the models perform similarly,
partly because both struggle with output format-
ting. Under the full structured-reasoning pipeline,
however, Mistral-24B reaches macro-F1 0.65 on
the validation set, compared with 0.51 for Gemma-
2-9B. This result suggests that reasoning prompts
can reduce formatting noise, while successful fac-
tual retrieval still depends on model capacity.
Mistral-24B performs better on long-tail entities
such as small islands, club-level stadiums, and less
prominent awards. Thus, in a closed-book set-
ting, a larger model may benefit more from such a
pipeline.

Run-to-run variance. Two minor sources of
variation affect our runs. First, awardWonBy uses
sampling (T = 0.7, six decade-scoped passes) to
diversify recall over long recipient lists, so its score
fluctuates slightly given only 10 validation awards.
Second, even under greedy decoding (T = 0.0) the
TPU v5e-8 is not bit-exact, because the accumula-
tion order of bfloat16 values differs across its eight
cores. Both effects are small—overall macro-F1
varies by about ±0.005—and do not change our
conclusions.
7 Conclusion
We presented the REAP system for the AKBC
Shared Task 2026 under a strict closed-book
setting with at most 32B parameters, no exter-
nal knowledge, and no model fine-tuning. The
system implements a unified two-stage pipeline
with Mistral-Small-24B-Instruct-2501, combining
relation-aware prompt engineering, a reasoning-
based empty-set gate, and direct parsing. It
achieves a macro-F1 of 0.65 on the validation set
and a macro-F1 of 0.62 on the official test set.
The results demonstrate that structured reasoning
can effectively elicit factual knowledge encoded in
model parameters for knowledge base construction.
Limitations
Despite its promising performance, our system has
several limitations: (i) its parametric knowledge
remains incomplete for very rare, long-tail enti-
ties; (ii) predictions for quantitative relations some-
times fall outside the 5% relative-tolerance thresh-
old because of retrieval or rounding errors; and (iii)
stochastic sampling for awardWonBy, together with
non-deterministic distributed computation on TPU
v5e-8, causes slight variation across runs. Among
the six relations, hasCapacity is the most chal-
lenging (test macro-F1 0.23): venues are frequently
confused with larger namesakes in the same city,
and even small numeric errors exceed the 5% tol-
erance.
